set.detail:
After Spartacus broke through Crassus' fortified line in Bruttium in winter 72/71, his army divided again; Crassus destroyed the Gallic and German breakaway force under Castus and Gannicus at a Lucanian lake. Meanwhile the Senate had recalled Pompey from Spain and Lucullus' brother Marcus Lucullus from Thrace, giving Crassus every reason to finish the war before they claimed the credit. Spartacus, harried by Crassus' cavalry, turned to fight in Lucania near the headwaters of the Silarus (Sele) river in spring 71.

Plutarch reports that before the battle Spartacus killed his horse, saying that if he won he would have many fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would not need one. He then tried to reach Crassus himself, killing two centurions, but was surrounded and cut down. His body was never found. Appian says that he was wounded in the thigh and fought on his knees. The slave army was destroyed; Appian puts the dead at a figure that cannot be trusted, but the result was decisive. About 6,000 prisoners were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome, a distance of some 200 km, as a deterrent.

Five thousand fugitives fled north and were intercepted in Etruria by Pompey, returning from Spain, who wrote to the Senate that while Crassus had defeated the slaves, he had torn out the war by the roots. The rivalry this provoked shaped their joint consulship of 70. Crassus received only an ovation, not a triumph, because the enemy were slaves, though he was allowed a laurel wreath instead of the usual myrtle.

The site has been placed near the modern town of Quaglietta in the upper Sele valley, or near Paestum; neither is certain. Spartacus' death ended the last great slave revolt of antiquity.
set.debate: The location in the upper Silarus valley is approximate; Appian's figure of 60,000 slaves killed is not credible.

scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)

set.detail:
Pompey and Crassus both stood for the consulship of 70 while still commanding armies outside Rome. Pompey, at thirty-five, had held no previous magistracy and was not even a senator; the Senate waived the requirements of the lex annalis. Crassus, who had held the praetorship, was legally qualified. Though rivals, they made a temporary alliance, and both were elected. Pompey celebrated his second triumph, for Spain, on 29 December 71, and appeared before the censors as an eques to report his military service, leading his horse through the Forum to great applause.

Their consulship dismantled the core of Sulla's settlement. A law of both consuls restored the tribunes' full powers, including legislative initiative, a cause Pompey had promised in his election speech and which the plebs had demanded since 78. The praetor Lucius Aurelius Cotta carried the lex Aurelia iudiciaria, dividing juries equally among senators, equites and tribuni aerarii. The censors, Gellius and Lentulus, the first since 86, expelled 64 senators and registered 910,000 citizens.

The year was marked by the trial of Verres and by public quarrels between the consuls. At the end of the year, Plutarch says, a Roman knight, Gaius Aurelius, reported that Jupiter had appeared to him in a dream ordering him to tell the consuls to be reconciled before laying down office. Crassus offered his hand to Pompey, and they parted publicly friends. Crassus had also celebrated by feasting the people at 10,000 tables and giving each citizen three months' grain.

The consulship showed how the two great commanders of the 70s could use popular measures to win influence. Neither took a province afterward. The restored tribunate became the instrument for Pompey's commands in 67 and 66, and their partnership prefigured the alliance of 60.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2nd ed. 2002)
Ward, Marcus Crassus and the Late Roman Republic (1977)

set.detail:
Gaius Verres had governed Sicily as propraetor for three years (73-71), extended because of the Spartacus war, and stripped the province systematically: manipulating the grain tithes, selling verdicts, extorting money from cities, and seizing works of art from temples and private houses, including the statue of Diana at Segesta and the silver of Sicilian families. The Sicilian communities, many of which had been clients of Cicero since his quaestorship at Lilybaeum in 75, asked him to prosecute under the extortion law. Verres was defended by Quintus Hortensius, the leading orator of the day and consul-elect for 69.

Verres' strategy was delay: if the trial could be pushed into 69, Hortensius would be consul, Quintus Metellus would preside over the extortion court, and a sympathetic jury could be drawn. His friends first tried to install a sham prosecutor, Quintus Caecilius Niger, whom Cicero defeated in a preliminary hearing (Divinatio in Caecilium). Cicero then gathered evidence in Sicily in fifty days. At the trial in August 70 he abandoned the usual long opening speech and presented his witnesses and documents immediately, speaking only briefly (the Actio prima). The evidence was overwhelming; after nine days Verres went into voluntary exile at Massilia without waiting for the verdict.

Cicero then published the five speeches of the Actio secunda, which he never delivered, a comprehensive indictment covering the grain tithes, the art thefts (De signis) and the crucifixion of the Roman citizen Gavius at Messana, who cried 'I am a Roman citizen' as he was flogged. The damages assessed were three million sesterces against the forty million Cicero claimed.

The case made Cicero the foremost orator in Rome, overtaking Hortensius, and occurred as jury reform was being debated; the lex Aurelia followed. Verres lived in exile until 43, when he was proscribed by Antony, allegedly for refusing to give up his Corinthian bronzes.

scholarship: Frazel, The Rhetoric of Cicero's In Verrem (2009)
Miles, Art as Plunder (2008)

set.detail:
In spring 69 Lucullus, having conquered Pontus, invaded Armenia because Tigranes II refused to hand over Mithridates. With only two legions and some 3,000 cavalry, around 12,000-15,000 men, he crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris and besieged Tigranocerta, the new royal capital Tigranes had founded and populated with Greeks and others deported from Cappadocia, Cilicia and Mesopotamia. Tigranes came to relieve it with an army the sources inflate to 250,000, including heavily armoured cataphract cavalry. Seeing the small Roman force, he quipped that it was too many for an embassy and too few for an army.

On 6 October 69, Lucullus, told that it was an unlucky day, the anniversary of Arausio, replied that he would make it a lucky one. He crossed the river and led two cohorts up a hill on the flank of the Armenian cataphracts, ordering his men to strike at the horses' legs and riders' thighs, the only unprotected parts. The cataphracts broke and rode back into their own infantry, and the Armenian army dissolved in panic. Tigranes fled, throwing away his diadem. Plutarch, following Lucullus' report, gives 100,000 Armenian infantry dead and only 5 Roman dead and 100 wounded. The Greek mercenaries in Tigranocerta then opened the gates; Lucullus took 8,000 talents in the royal treasury and repatriated the deported populations.

The victory was among the most remarkable of Roman arms against odds, and Livy noted that never had Romans faced so great a disparity. But it overextended Lucullus. His soldiers, many of them the Valeriani of 86 who had served for fifteen years, resented his discipline and his restraint on looting. His subsequent march toward Artaxata in 68 ended in mutiny.
set.debate: Site of Tigranocerta (Arzan versus Silvan) and the size of Tigranes' army. The site of Tigranocerta is disputed (Arzan, Silvan or near Diyarbakır); casualty figures are propaganda.

scholarship: Sinclair, Eastern Turkey: An Architectural and Archaeological Survey III (1989) on the site

set.detail:
Piracy in the Mediterranean had grown to crisis proportions by the 60s. Cilician and Cretan pirates, swollen by refugees from the Mithridatic wars, had sacked over 400 cities, kidnapped Roman magistrates and the young Caesar, raided Ostia and burned a consular fleet there, and choked the grain supply, causing price rises and riots in Rome. Earlier commands, by Marcus Antonius in 102, Servilius Isauricus in 78-74 and Antonius Creticus in 74-71, had failed to solve the problem.

In January 67 the tribune Aulus Gabinius proposed to appoint a single commander of consular rank for three years with authority over the whole Mediterranean and its coasts up to fifty miles inland, equal to that of provincial governors (imperium aequum), with fifteen (later twenty-four) legates of praetorian rank, 500 ships, 120,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry, and the right to draw funds from the treasury. No name was mentioned, but everyone understood it was Pompey. The Senate opposed the bill almost unanimously; the consul Piso threatened that Pompey would end like Romulus, murdered by senators. A tribune who vetoed was threatened with deposition, as Octavius had been in 133, and withdrew. Catulus' speech against the bill was answered by the crowd. Caesar alone among senators supported it. On the day the law passed, the price of grain fell immediately.

Pompey divided the sea into thirteen districts, each under a legate, swept the western Mediterranean in forty days, and then in forty-nine days more cornered the pirates in Cilicia, destroying their main fleet at Coracesium. Some 20,000 captives were resettled as farmers at Soli (renamed Pompeiopolis), Dyme and elsewhere.

The lex Gabinia was the most important constitutional precedent of the late Republic. It created an empire-wide command for one man by popular vote against the Senate, foreshadowing the powers Augustus would hold. Cicero, then praetor, supported Pompey in 66; later historians saw it as the start of the slide to monarchy.
set.debate: Whether Pompey's imperium was 'equal' (aequum, Velleius) or superior (maius) to governors' is disputed. Whether Pompey's imperium was 'aequum' with or 'maius' than governors' (Velleius vs Tacitus) is disputed.

scholarship: de Souza, Piracy in the Graeco-Roman World (1999)

set.detail:
By the end of 67 Lucullus' position in the East had collapsed: his army had mutinied after Nisibis, Mithridates had recovered Pontus and destroyed a Roman force under Triarius at Zela, and the province of Asia was in danger. Lucullus' political enemies at Rome, particularly the equestrian tax-farmers whose profits he had curbed by limiting interest in Asia, had already stripped him of Asia, Cilicia and Bithynia. The tribune Gaius Manilius proposed in early 66 that Pompey, who had just completed the pirate war and was still in Cilicia with large forces, should be given command of the war against Mithridates and Tigranes, with the provinces of Cilicia and Bithynia and authority to make war and peace.

The proposal was supported by Caesar and by Cicero, then praetor, in his first political speech from the rostra, De imperio Cn. Pompei (also called Pro lege Manilia). Cicero argued that the war threatened the revenues of Asia and the property of the equites, and that Pompey had the four qualities of the perfect general: military knowledge, courage, authority and good fortune. Catulus and Hortensius opposed it, as with the Gabinian law, but the bill passed unanimously by the tribes.

Pompey received the news, Plutarch says, with a show of reluctance, complaining that he would never be allowed to rest, which his friends found insufferable hypocrisy. He met Lucullus at Danala, annulled his arrangements, and took over his army, leaving him only 1,600 men for his triumph, which was delayed until 63.

The law gave Pompey an unprecedented accumulation of power: authority over the eastern sea by the lex Gabinia and over the eastern land war by the lex Manilia, with freedom to make treaties. In the next four years he used it to reorganise the entire Roman East.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)
Steel, Cicero, Rhetoric and Empire (2001)

set.detail:
In spring 66 Pompey, with perhaps 50,000 men, invaded Lesser Armenia, where Mithridates, now with only some 30,000 foot and 3,000 horse, practised a scorched-earth retreat, refusing battle. After a period of manoeuvre, Pompey trapped him in a defile near the Lycus river at a place later called Nicopolis, near Dasteira. He attacked at night, with the moon behind the Romans, so that the Pontic soldiers misjudged the distance of their enemies from the length of their shadows and threw their javelins short.

The Pontic army was cut to pieces in the darkness and confusion; the sources give 10,000 killed and the camp captured. Mithridates broke through with 800 horsemen, of whom only three stayed with him, including his concubine Hypsicratea, who rode and fought dressed as a man, and whom he called Hypsicrates. He gathered survivors at the fortress of Sinoria, distributed treasure and poison among his followers, and fled toward Armenia. Tigranes, now suspicious of him and facing his own son's revolt, refused him entry and set a price of 100 talents on his head. Mithridates escaped instead to Colchis, wintering at Dioscurias.

Pompey founded the city of Nicopolis (Victory City) on the battlefield and settled it with his veterans and wounded, one of several foundations that made him the greatest city-founder since Alexander. He then turned on Armenia, where Tigranes submitted at Artaxata.

The battle effectively ended Mithridates' power as a major military threat, though he would continue to resist from the Bosporus for three more years.
set.debate: The exact location (near Koyulhisar or Purk in the upper Lycus valley) is uncertain.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)
Mayor, The Poison King (2010)

set.detail:
The Seleucid kingdom had disintegrated by the 80s into a patchwork of rival claimants, autonomous cities, Arab dynasts and Judaean and Ituraean principalities. From 83 to 69 Tigranes II of Armenia ruled Syria from Antioch. After Lucullus' victory at Tigranocerta, the young Antiochus XIII, son of Antiochus X, was installed at Antioch, but he was challenged by Philip II and the Arab dynasts of Emesa and Chalcis, and the region remained chaotic.

In 64 Pompey, arriving in Syria from the Caucasus, refused to recognise Antiochus XIII, reportedly saying that a king who could not defend his kingdom against Tigranes could not defend it against the Arabs and Jews either, and that Rome would not leave it to be plundered. He annexed Syria as a Roman province, ending the dynasty founded by Seleucus I in 312. Antiochus was killed soon after by the Emesene dynast Sampsiceramus. Pompey organised the new province with its capital at Antioch, confirming the freedom of many Greek cities, restoring cities destroyed by the Jews (such as Gadara, rebuilt for his freedman Demetrius) and forming the league of the Decapolis.

Pompey surrounded the province with client rulers: Sampsiceramus at Emesa, Ptolemy son of Mennaeus in Ituraea, Abgar of Osroene, Antiochus I of Commagene, and the Hasmonean high priest Hyrcanus in Judaea. Aemilius Scaurus was left as governor with two legions.

The annexation made Rome a direct neighbour of Parthia and of the Arab and Nabataean world, and brought it to the borders of Egypt. Syria became one of the most important provinces of the empire, with a large garrison, and the base for Crassus' disastrous campaign of 53. Modern scholars debate whether Pompey's decision was driven by strategy, by the fiscal interests of the publicani, or by the desire for glory.

scholarship: Sartre, The Middle East under Rome (2005)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

set.detail:
The rival Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II brought their dispute to Pompey at Damascus in spring 63, along with a delegation of the Jewish people who asked for the abolition of the monarchy. Pompey postponed his decision; Aristobulus left in anger and fortified Jerusalem. Pompey marched on him, arrested him when he came out to negotiate, but Aristobulus' supporters held the Temple Mount, while Hyrcanus' party opened the city gates.

Pompey besieged the Temple for three months, bringing siege engines from Tyre and filling the deep ditch on the north side. Josephus reports that the Romans worked on the earthworks on the Sabbath, when the defenders would not fight except to repel a direct attack. The Temple fell in autumn 63, according to Josephus on the Day of Atonement, perhaps a misunderstanding of a fast day. Faustus Sulla, son of the dictator, was the first over the wall. Some 12,000 Jews were killed; priests continued their sacrifices as they were cut down.

Pompey entered the Holy of Holies with his officers, an act of sacrilege remembered with horror, but he took nothing from the Temple's treasure of 2,000 talents and ordered the sanctuary cleansed and worship resumed the next day. Cicero praised his restraint. He restored Hyrcanus as high priest without the royal title, reduced Judaea's territory by freeing the Greek cities of the coast and Decapolis, imposed tribute, and took Aristobulus and his children to walk in his triumph.

The capture marked the end of Judaean independence under the Hasmoneans and the beginning of Roman domination. The Psalms of Solomon, a Jewish text composed soon after, lament the 'man alien to our race' who profaned the Temple and describe Pompey's death in Egypt as divine punishment.
set.debate: Whether the fast day is the Day of Atonement, a Sabbath, or a confusion by Strabo, whom Josephus follows. Date of the fall (Day of Atonement or another fast) is debated; Dio dates it to the Sabbath.

scholarship: Schürer, History of the Jewish People I (rev. 1973)
Smallwood, The Jews under Roman Rule (1976)

set.detail:
After fleeing from the Lycus, Mithridates crossed the Caucasus to the Cimmerian Bosporus in 65, where he forced his son Machares, who had made peace with Rome, to kill himself, and re-established his rule from Panticapaeum. Even at nearly seventy he planned a grandiose invasion of Italy by land, through the Scythian and Celtic lands and over the Alps, like Hannibal. His subjects, crushed by taxation, and his army, alarmed by his plans, wavered.

In 63 his son Pharnaces led a revolt with the army and the people of Panticapaeum. Mithridates, besieged in his palace, tried to poison himself and his two young daughters, who had been betrothed to the kings of Egypt and Cyprus. The poison killed the girls but not him, because, according to tradition, he had made himself immune by taking small doses of poison throughout his life. He then asked his Gallic bodyguard, Bituitus, to kill him with a sword. Pharnaces sent his father's embalmed body to Pompey at Amisus as a token of loyalty; Pompey had it buried in the royal tombs at Sinope.

News of the death reached Pompey near Jericho, where his soldiers celebrated with sacrifices and feasts. In Rome the consul Cicero proposed a ten-day thanksgiving. Pharnaces was rewarded with the Bosporan kingdom as a friend and ally of Rome.

Mithridates had fought Rome for over twenty-five years, the most dangerous enemy since Hannibal in Cicero's view. He became a legend: the polyglot king who spoke twenty-two languages, the toxicologist whose universal antidote, mithridatium, was copied by doctors into the eighteenth century. Modern historians emphasise his skill in exploiting Greek resentment of Rome and his creation of a Black Sea empire.
set.debate: Whether Mithridates' immunity to poison was real or legend is unknowable; his age at death (c. 69-72) is uncertain.

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

set.detail:
Between 66 and 62 Pompey reorganised the entire Roman East under the authority of the lex Manilia, making treaties and decisions without the usual senatorial commission. The result was the framework of Roman rule in the region for over a century. New provinces were created: Bithynia-Pontus, combining the western half of Pontus with the Bithynian bequest and divided into eleven city-territories; Syria, ending the Seleucid dynasty; and an enlarged Cilicia. Crete was annexed separately by Metellus.

Around the provinces Pompey placed a ring of client kings and dynasts: Deiotarus in Galatia and Lesser Armenia, Ariobarzanes in Cappadocia (with additional territory), Tigranes in a reduced Armenia, Antiochus of Commagene, Pharnaces in the Bosporus, Archelaus as priest-ruler at Comana, Hyrcanus as high priest in Judaea, Arab dynasts at Emesa and Osroene. He founded or refounded some thirty-nine cities, including Nicopolis on the Lycus, Pompeiopolis in Paphlagonia and Cilicia, Magnopolis and Megalopolis, and settled 20,000 former pirates.

Financially the settlement was transformative. Plutarch reports that Pompey raised the state's annual revenues from 50 million to 85 million denarii (from 200 to 340 million sesterces), an increase of 70 per cent, and brought 20,000 talents into the treasury. His soldiers received 6,000 sesterces each, officers far more; Pompey himself became the richest man in Rome, with clients throughout the East.

The settlement's ratification became the central political issue of 61-59. Lucullus, whose arrangements Pompey had annulled, and Cato obstructed it in the Senate, demanding that each act be examined individually. Pompey's failure to have it approved drove him into the alliance with Caesar and Crassus, and Caesar ratified it en bloc in 59. Modern assessments credit Pompey with administrative ability and a coherent vision.

scholarship: Dreizehnter, 'Pompeius als Städtegründer', Chiron 5 (1975)

set.detail:
Marcus Tullius Cicero was elected consul for 63 at the first legal age, 42, as a novus homo, the first from a non-senatorial family since 94, winning all centuries. His victory over Catiline and Gaius Antonius was due partly to fear of Catiline among the optimates, who backed Cicero as the lesser evil. He bought off his colleague Antonius by exchanging provinces, giving him rich Macedonia.

Cicero's consulship began with his opposition to the agrarian bill of the tribune Publius Servilius Rullus, which proposed a commission of ten with sweeping powers to buy and distribute land, financed by the sale of public property and Pompey's conquests; Cicero's three speeches persuaded the people to reject it. He defended Gaius Rabirius, an elderly senator charged with treason for the killing of Saturninus in 100, in a case engineered by Caesar and Labienus to challenge the legitimacy of the senatus consultum ultimum. He also opposed a proposal to restore the political rights of the sons of the proscribed, and passed a law against bribery, the lex Tullia de ambitu.

The dominating event was the conspiracy of Catiline, defeated at the elections for 62 in July. Through informants, especially Fulvia, mistress of the conspirator Quintus Curius, Cicero followed the plot, obtained the senatus consultum ultimum on 21 October, and drove Catiline out of Rome with the First Catilinarian on 8 November. He arrested the conspirators in Rome on 3 December with the evidence of the Allobroges and had five executed on 5 December. He was hailed as pater patriae by Catulus.

Cicero regarded his consulship as the summit of his life and wrote about it endlessly, in Greek and Latin prose and verse ('O fortunatam natam me consule Romam'), exposing himself to ridicule. The execution of citizens without trial would bring his exile in 58.

scholarship: Habicht, Cicero the Politician (1990)

set.detail:
On 3 December 63, after the arrest of the Allobrogian envoys at the Milvian Bridge with letters from the conspirators, Cicero summoned Lentulus Sura, a praetor and former consul, Cethegus, Statilius, Gabinius Capito and Caeparius to the Senate, where they were confronted with their seals and handwriting and confessed. They were placed in the custody of leading senators. On 5 December the Senate met in the temple of Concord to decide their fate.

The consul-designate Decimus Junius Silanus proposed the 'ultimate penalty', and the consulars followed. When it came to Caesar, praetor-designate, he argued that execution of citizens without trial violated the laws, notably Gaius Gracchus' lex de capite civis, and proposed life imprisonment in the Italian municipia with confiscation of property. His speech swayed many, including Silanus, who reinterpreted his proposal. Cicero made his Fourth Catilinarian, leaving the decision to the Senate while hinting at his own preference. Then the young tribune-designate Marcus Porcius Cato spoke, denouncing the conspirators and Caesar, and demanding execution in the ancestral manner. The Senate voted for death.

That evening Cicero personally escorted Lentulus to the Tullianum, the underground prison at the foot of the Capitol, where the five were strangled by the executioners. Cicero announced to the crowd 'vixerunt', they have lived. He was escorted home by torchlight, and Catulus hailed him as father of the fatherland.

Sallust's account, with its paired speeches of Caesar and Cato, contrasting clemency with severity, is the most famous Roman historical set piece. The question of legality followed Cicero: Metellus Nepos prevented his farewell speech on 31 December, and Clodius' law of 58 drove him into exile. The episode crystallised the debate over the senatus consultum ultimum.

scholarship: Drummond, Law, Politics and Power: Sallust and the Execution of the Catilinarian Conspirators (1995)
Levick, Catiline (2015)

set.detail:
Pompey's third triumph, celebrated on 28 and 29 September 61, his forty-fifth birthday, was the most magnificent the city had seen. Placards listed the conquered peoples: Pontus, Armenia, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia, Media, Colchis, Iberia, Albania, Syria, Cilicia, Mesopotamia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Judaea, Arabia and the pirates. Inscriptions boasted that he had captured 1,000 fortresses, 900 cities and 800 pirate ships, founded 39 cities, and raised the state's revenues by 70 per cent.

In the procession were 324 captives, including Tigranes the Younger with his wife and daughter, Aristobulus II and his children, the sister and five sons of Mithridates, Scythian women and the hostages of the Iberians and Albanians. Images of Mithridates and Tigranes were carried, along with a portrait of Pompey made of pearls, which Pliny disparaged, a golden statue of Mithridates eight cubits high, the king's gaming board made of two precious stones, and his collection of engraved gems (dactyliotheca), which Pompey dedicated on the Capitol. Pompey wore a cloak said to have belonged to Alexander the Great.

He did not, however, execute the captives, as was customary, but sent them home at public expense, except those of royal blood. The triumph celebrated victory over three continents, Africa (82), Europe (71) and Asia (61), and Pompey was presented as a new Alexander.

Yet the triumph came at the moment of Pompey's political weakness. Having disbanded his army, he faced obstruction from Lucullus, Cato and Metellus Celer, who refused to ratify his eastern acts or provide land for his veterans. Within months he was looking for allies, which led him to Caesar. The spoils financed his theatre complex in the Campus Martius.

scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Östenberg, Staging the World (2009)

set.detail:
In 60 the three most powerful men in Rome were each frustrated by the Senate. Pompey could not get his eastern settlement ratified or land for his veterans. Crassus could not win a remission for the Asian tax-farmers, who had overbid for their contract. Caesar, returning from Spain, had been forced by Cato's filibuster to give up his triumph to stand for the consulship, and the Senate had assigned the consuls of 59 the 'woods and paths of Italy' as provinces to deny him a command. Caesar reconciled Pompey and Crassus, enemies since 70, and the three agreed, in Suetonius' words, that nothing should be done in the state that displeased any one of them.

The pact was informal and secret at first; the term 'triumvirate' is modern, by analogy with the legal Second Triumvirate of 43. Contemporaries called it a factio or regnum; Varro wrote a pamphlet titled Tricaranus, 'the three-headed monster'. Cicero was invited to join but declined. Its date is uncertain: probably after Caesar's election in summer 60, though some date it to December 60 or the start of 59.

During Caesar's consulship of 59 the alliance passed legislation for all three: land for Pompey's veterans, ratification of his acts, remission of a third of the Asian contract for Crassus' clients, and for Caesar a five-year command in Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul (later Transalpine Gaul too). It was sealed by Pompey's marriage to Caesar's daughter Julia.

Ancient writers from Asinius Pollio onward dated the start of the civil wars to 60, not 49. Horace's ode to Pollio opens with 'the civil commotion from the consulship of Metellus'. Modern scholars debate whether it was a revolutionary conspiracy or a temporary alliance; Gruen argued the Republic continued to function, but most see it as fatally undermining senatorial government.
set.debate: Date (60 or early 59) and nature: a conspiracy against the Republic (Syme) or an ad hoc alliance produced by senatorial obstruction (Gruen). The date of the pact (summer 60, December 60, or early 59) and its character are debated.

scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

set.detail:
Caesar entered office on 1 January 59 with Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, Cato's son-in-law, as his colleague. He began conciliatorily, publishing the acta of the Senate and offering his agrarian bill for senatorial discussion. When Cato filibustered it, Caesar had him led off to prison, then released him as senators followed; he took the bill directly to the people. At the assembly Bibulus tried to veto and was driven from the Forum, his fasces broken and a basket of dung emptied over his head. Thereafter Bibulus stayed home 'watching the skies' for omens, a procedure which, his supporters claimed, invalidated all subsequent legislation.

Caesar's legislation was extensive: the agrarian law and a second law for Campania; ratification of Pompey's eastern acts; the remission of a third of the Asian tax contract; recognition of Ptolemy XII as king for a reported 6,000 talents; a comprehensive extortion law, the lex Julia de repetundis, which remained the basis of the law for centuries; and through the tribune Vatinius his own five-year command in Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum, to which the Senate added Transalpine Gaul. He also arranged Clodius' adoption into the plebs, opening his way to the tribunate.

The year brought the alliance into the open: Pompey married Julia, Caesar married Calpurnia, daughter of the consul-designate Piso. Public opinion turned against the dynasts during the summer; at the Ludi Apollinares the actor Diphilus was cheered for the line 'by our misery you are Great', and Pompey was booed.

The legality of Caesar's acts, passed in defiance of a colleague's obnuntiatio and veto, was challenged immediately by the praetors Memmius and Domitius. It was the source of Caesar's fear of prosecution if he returned as a private citizen, and hence of his insistence on a second consulship directly from his command in 49.

scholarship: Taylor, 'The dating of major legislation and elections in Caesar's first consulship', Historia 17 (1968)

set.detail:
Caesar's first agrarian law provided land for Pompey's veterans and for the urban poor, especially fathers of three or more children. To avoid the controversies of the Gracchan laws, it excluded the Campanian ager publicus, the most valuable remaining public land, and provided that land be purchased from willing sellers at the valuation of the last census, funded by the revenues of Pompey's conquests. A commission of twenty, including Pompey and Crassus, with a sub-board of five, administered it. All senators and candidates for office were required to swear to uphold the law; Cato and Metellus Celer resisted but finally swore.

In May a second law, the lex Campana, distributed the Campanian land after all, settling some 20,000 citizens with three or more children there and refounding Capua as a colony. This ended the state's rental income from the land, which had been one of its most reliable revenues, provoking Cicero's lament that the treasury had lost its most important estate.

The laws were passed by the assembly in defiance of Bibulus' obstruction, and Caesar's opponents regarded them as invalid. Their implementation was slow: in 56 Cicero proposed to debate the Campanian land in the Senate, a move that helped provoke the conference of Luca.

The agrarian laws showed that land for veterans had become a central political issue, requiring a powerful patron. The same need recurred after Caesar's civil war, with his colonies, and after Philippi, with the triumvirs' confiscations. Caesar's laws, by paying for land rather than confiscating it, were the most moderate of all these schemes.

scholarship: Gelzer, Caesar: Politician and Statesman (1968)

set.detail:
The tribune Publius Vatinius, Caesar's agent, carried a law in spring 59 giving Caesar the provinces of Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years, until 1 March 54, with three legions and the right to appoint his legates. The Senate, on Pompey's motion, then added Transalpine Gaul, whose governor Metellus Celer had died, with a fourth legion, to be renewed annually. Cato warned the Senate that it was installing a tyrant in the citadel.

The command was extraordinary in its length and in being conferred by the people rather than the Senate, following the precedents of Pompey's commands of 67 and 66. It gave Caesar an army and the chance to rival Pompey's military glory. Its strategic purpose is debated. Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul suggest that Caesar may originally have planned a war against Burebista's Dacians in the Danube basin; the Helvetian migration in March 58 offered a pretext in the west instead.

The command was extended for another five years by the lex Pompeia Licinia of 55, after the conference at Luca. The terminal date of the extended command became the legal crux of the crisis of 50-49: Caesar's opponents argued that it expired on 1 March 50 and sought to recall him then; Caesar claimed the right to keep it until he could take up a second consulship in 48.

Vatinius' tribunate also produced laws on the extortion court and on jurors' challenges. Cicero, who later attacked him in In Vatinium (56), defended him in 54 at Pompey's insistence. The lex Vatinia is the foundation of Caesar's career.
set.debate: The 'Rechtsfrage': the legal end-date of Caesar's command (Mommsen, Balsdon, Gruen) is unresolved. The original plan for a Danubian campaign against Burebista is a modern hypothesis based on the inclusion of Illyricum.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)
Pelling, Plutarch: Caesar (2011), commentary
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

set.detail:
Publius Clodius Pulcher, tribune from 10 December 59, carried a package of laws in January 58 that made him master of the streets. The first made the monthly grain ration free for the first time, at an annual cost the treasury put at a fifth of revenues; administration was entrusted to Clodius' client Sextus Cloelius. The second restored the collegia, the neighbourhood and trade associations suppressed in 64, and permitted new ones, which Clodius organised by district (vicus) as political cells. The third restricted the use of obnuntiatio, the announcement of unfavourable omens to block assemblies, which Bibulus had used against Caesar. The fourth limited the censors' power to expel senators without a trial and the agreement of both censors.

Clodius followed these with the lex de capite civis that exiled Cicero, the law annexing Cyprus and sending Cato to administer it, and laws assigning the consuls Piso and Gabinius rich provinces, Macedonia and Syria. He also restored the cult of Isis, and supported the cults of the Compitalia.

The free grain distribution created a vast clientele: some 320,000 recipients by 46, when Caesar reduced them. It also overstrained supply, and in 57 shortages and riots led to Pompey's appointment as curator of the grain supply for five years.

Modern scholars (Tatum, Benner, Vanderbroeck) have reassessed Clodius as a skilful popularis politician rather than a mere gang leader. His organisation of the urban plebs through the collegia and the grain distribution gave him lasting power independent of the triumvirs, whom he defied as often as he served.

scholarship: Tatum, The Patrician Tribune: Publius Clodius Pulcher (1999)
Benner, Die Politik des P. Clodius Pulcher (1987)

set.detail:
Early in 58 Clodius carried a law outlawing anyone who had put a Roman citizen to death without trial. It named no one, but everyone understood it was aimed at Cicero for the execution of the Catilinarians. Cicero put on mourning, and the equites and many senators did the same; the consuls Piso and Gabinius forbade it. Pompey, whom Cicero had counted on, withdrew to his Alban villa and avoided him; Caesar, waiting outside the city with his army before leaving for Gaul, offered Cicero a post on his staff, which he refused, and stated that he opposed the executions but disapproved of retroactive legislation.

Cicero left Rome in March 58, the night before a second law named him personally, forbidding him fire and water within 400 miles of Italy and confiscating his property. His house on the Palatine was demolished and a shrine to Libertas built on part of the site; his villas at Tusculum and Formiae were plundered. He went to Thessalonica, then Dyrrachium, in a state of despair recorded in letters to Atticus and to his wife Terentia, writing that he wished he had died.

His recall was engineered by the tribunes Milo and Sestius with Pompey's backing, against Clodius' violent opposition. After a riot on 23 January 57 in which Quintus Cicero was left for dead, the Senate met in the temple of Honos and Virtus, and a law passed by the centuriate assembly on 4 August 57, with voters from all Italy, recalled him. He landed at Brundisium on 5 August and returned to Rome in triumph on 4 September.

The exile marked the limits of Cicero's political power and haunted his later writings. His speeches after his return, Post reditum, De domo sua, Pro Sestio, construct an image of the exile as a martyrdom for the Republic.

scholarship: Kaster, Cicero: Speech on Behalf of Publius Sestius (2006)
Nicholson, Cicero's Return from Exile (1992)

set.detail:
Blocked at Geneva, the Helvetii took the northern route through the Jura pass into Sequanian and Aeduan territory. Caesar caught their rearguard, the Tigurini, crossing the Arar (Saône) and destroyed it, then followed the main column for two weeks. Short of grain because his Aeduan allies, influenced by Dumnorix, were withholding supplies, he turned toward the Aeduan capital Bibracte (Mont Beuvray), eighteen miles away. The Helvetii, thinking he was retreating, attacked him near Bibracte in early summer 58.

Caesar drew up his four veteran legions in three lines on a hillside, with the two new legions and auxiliaries guarding the baggage on the summit. He sent away all horses, including his own, so that no one could flee. The Helvetii, in a dense phalanx, charged uphill; the Roman pila pierced their overlapping shields, pinning them together, and many threw their shields away. The legions drove them back to a hill a mile off, where the Boii and Tulingi, 15,000 strong, attacked the Roman flank; Caesar turned his third line to face them. The fighting went on from midday until evening, ending at the Helvetian wagon laager, which was defended through the night.

Some 130,000 survivors fled to the Lingones; Caesar forbade the Lingones to help them, and the Helvetii surrendered. He ordered them to return to their land and rebuild their towns, so that the Germans would not occupy it, and settled the Boii among the Aedui. According to Caesar's figures, of 368,000 who set out, 110,000 returned.

The site has been sought near Montmort, south of Bibracte, where in the nineteenth century Napoleon III's excavations claimed to find Roman camps. Caesar's numbers are not credible, but the battle established his reputation and Rome's dominance over central Gaul.
set.debate: Battlefield proposed near Montmort or Armecy; Caesar's population figures are probably inflated. The site (Montmort or elsewhere near Bibracte) and Caesar's numbers are disputed.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)

set.detail:
After the Helvetian campaign a council of Gallic leaders, led by the Aeduan Diviciacus, asked Caesar to free them from Ariovistus, the Suebic king who had defeated the Aedui at Magetobriga and now held a third of Sequanian land with 120,000 Germans, and demanded another third for the Harudes. Ariovistus, recognised by the Senate as 'king and friend' in 59, refused Caesar's summons, replying that Gaul was his province as the Narbonensis was Rome's. Caesar occupied Vesontio, overcame a panic in his army, and marched into Alsace.

A parley between Caesar and Ariovistus on horseback broke down when German horsemen attacked Caesar's escort; Ariovistus told Caesar that many Roman nobles would thank him for Caesar's death. Ariovistus then held two Roman envoys prisoner. For days he avoided battle; prisoners told Caesar that German wise women had forbidden fighting before the new moon. Caesar forced the issue in September 58 by marching on the German camp. The Germans formed up by tribes, their wagons behind them with the women imploring them not to surrender them to slavery.

The fighting was so close that the legionaries had no time to throw pila. The Roman right under Caesar routed the German left, but the German right pressed hard on the Roman left until Publius Crassus, commanding the cavalry, sent the third line to its relief. The Germans fled to the Rhine, some fifty miles away (Plutarch says five); Ariovistus escaped in a boat but his two wives and a daughter died, and the Roman envoys were recovered.

The battle, probably fought in the plain of Alsace near Mulhouse or Cernay, ended German expansion west of the Rhine and gave Caesar control of eastern Gaul. He wintered his legions among the Sequani, a sign that he intended to stay.
set.debate: Site disputed, probably near Cernay or Mulhouse; whether Caesar's provocation was legal was challenged in Rome. The site lies somewhere in the upper Alsace plain; the distance to the Rhine (five or fifty miles) varies between Plutarch and Caesar's manuscripts.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Christ, 'Caesar und Ariovist', Chiron 4 (1974)

set.detail:
In 57, after the Belgic coalition broke up at the Axona, Caesar marched against the Nervii, the most warlike of the Belgae, who banned wine and luxuries and refused to negotiate. With the Atrebates and Viromandui they waited in the forest on the far bank of the Sabis (probably the Selle, or the Sambre) for Caesar's column. Informed by deserters that each legion marched separated by its baggage, they planned to strike the first legion as it reached camp. Caesar had in fact changed his order of march, with six legions together in front, then all the baggage, then two new legions.

As the legions began fortifying the camp, the Nervii burst from the woods and across the river with incredible speed, scattering the cavalry and reaching the Roman lines before the soldiers could put on helmets or remove shield covers. The army fought in improvised groups. On the left, the Ninth and Tenth legions under Labienus drove the Atrebates back across the river; in the centre, the Eighth and Eleventh beat the Viromandui; but on the right, the Twelfth and Seventh were surrounded and nearly all their centurions killed, and the Nervii captured the camp. Caesar seized a shield from a soldier and went to the front line, calling centurions by name and ordering the ranks to open so they could use their swords.

The tide turned when Labienus sent the Tenth back from the enemy camp and the two rear legions arrived with the baggage. The Nervii fought to the last, standing on the piles of their own dead to throw weapons. Caesar claims that of 60,000 fighting men only 500 survived, and of 600 senators three; the Nervii nevertheless revolted again in 54.

The battle was Caesar's closest call in Gaul, and his narrative of it is a masterpiece of self-presentation. The Senate decreed a fifteen-day supplicatio, the longest ever.
set.debate: The river is identified with the Selle near Saulzoir by many, others prefer the Sambre near Maubeuge.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Lendon, 'The rhetoric of combat', Classical Antiquity 18 (1999)

set.detail:
By spring 56 the alliance of 60 was fraying. Pompey and Crassus were at odds, Clodius was harassing Pompey, and the optimates were attacking Caesar's acts: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, a candidate for the consulship of 55, promised to strip Caesar of his command, and Cicero, on 5 April, proposed that the Senate review the Campanian land law. Caesar, wintering in Cisalpine Gaul, met Crassus at Ravenna and then Pompey at Luca (Lucca), the southernmost town of his province, in mid-April. Over 120 lictors and some 200 senators are said to have gathered there.

The three renewed their alliance on new terms. Pompey and Crassus would hold a second joint consulship in 55, then receive five-year provinces, Spain for Pompey, Syria for Crassus; Caesar's command in Gaul would be extended for five years. Their supporters would delay the elections of 56 so that they could be held under a sympathetic interrex. Pompey also obliged Cicero to cease his attacks; Cicero wrote his 'palinode', the speech De provinciis consularibus supporting Caesar's continued command, and thereafter defended the dynasts' allies.

The plan was carried out. Violence and obstruction delayed the elections until January 55, when Pompey and Crassus were elected after their supporters attacked Domitius and wounded Cato. The tribune Gaius Trebonius carried the lex Trebonia giving them their provinces, and they carried the lex Pompeia Licinia extending Caesar's command.

The conference demonstrated that the dynasts could decide the allocation of consulships and provinces privately. Modern scholarship (Gruen, Luibheid) has questioned how far Luca was a formal 'conference' rather than a series of meetings, and whether the full plan was settled there.

scholarship: Luibheid, 'The Luca conference', CPh 65 (1970)
Gruen, 'Pompey, the Roman aristocracy, and the conference of Luca', Historia 18 (1969)

set.detail:
After the delayed elections in January 55 brought Pompey and Crassus their second joint consulship, the tribune Gaius Trebonius proposed that they receive provinces for five years: Pompey both Spains, Crassus Syria, with the right to raise troops and make war and peace. The tribunes Gaius Ateius Capito and Publius Aquillius Gallus opposed the bill. Cato spoke for two hours until he was dragged away, and in the riot several people were killed and Aquillius was beaten. Pompey reportedly returned from the assembly with his toga spattered with blood, and the sight of it, Plutarch says, caused his pregnant wife Julia to miscarry.

Soon after, the consuls carried the lex Pompeia Licinia extending Caesar's command in Gaul for five more years, probably to 1 March 50, though the terminal date became the subject of dispute. They also passed laws against bribery (the lex Licinia de sodaliciis), on jury selection, and Pompey a sumptuary law that he soon withdrew.

Pompey did not go to Spain. Instead he governed it through legates, Afranius and Petreius, while remaining near Rome with his imperium, outside the city, from where he also exercised his cura annonae; this was a novel arrangement that anticipated imperial governance of provinces by legates. Crassus left for Syria in November 55, cursed by Ateius at the city gate.

The lex Trebonia created a balance of three great commands, Gaul, Spain and Syria, that lasted until Crassus' death at Carrhae in 53 removed one of its pillars. Trebonius became one of Caesar's legates in Gaul, commanded the siege of Massilia in 49, and was one of the assassins of 44.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)
Ward, Marcus Crassus and the Late Roman Republic (1977)

set.detail:
Pompey's theatre, dedicated in 55 during his second consulship, was the first permanent stone theatre in Rome. Earlier theatres had been temporary wooden structures, for the Senate had repeatedly blocked permanent ones as a threat to public morals; in 154 the censors' stone theatre had been demolished on Scipio Nasica's motion. Pompey circumvented this by building a temple to Venus Victrix at the top of the auditorium, so that the seats became, as Tertullian later mocked, steps leading to the shrine.

The complex, financed by the spoils of the East, stood on the southern Campus Martius. The cavea, about 150 metres in diameter, seated some 10,000 to 17,000 (the 40,000 in Pliny's text may be corrupt or count standing room). Behind the stage a vast colonnaded garden, the Porticus Pompeiana, about 180 by 135 metres, held a park of plane trees, fountains, and a museum of statues and paintings, including fourteen statues of the nations Pompey had conquered by the sculptor Coponius. At the far end stood the Curia Pompeia, a hall for Senate meetings, where Caesar was killed in 44 at the foot of Pompey's statue.

Dedication games included musical and gymnastic contests, plays in which 600 mules carried spoils on stage in Accius' Clytemnestra, and the beast hunts with elephants that turned the crowd against Pompey. Cicero, in a letter to Marcus Marius, found the shows tasteless.

The theatre's curved outline survives in the street plan around Via di Grotta Pinta and Campo de' Fiori, and its substructures in the basements of buildings. It was restored by Augustus, Tiberius and later emperors and was still in use under Theodoric. The Severan Marble Plan shows its layout.
set.debate: The seating capacity is uncertain; recent estimates range from 10,000 to 25,000.

scholarship: Gagliardo and Packer, 'A new look at Pompey's theater', AJA 110 (2006)

set.detail:
In winter 56/55 two Germanic peoples, the Usipetes and Tencteri, driven from their lands by the Suebi, crossed the lower Rhine into the territory of the Menapii, perhaps 430,000 people by Caesar's count, including women and children. They sought land in Gaul, and some Gallic states invited them. In spring 55 Caesar marched against them. Their envoys asked for land or permission to settle; Caesar told them to settle among the Ubii across the Rhine and agreed to a short truce while they consulted.

During the truce, 800 German cavalry attacked 5,000 of Caesar's Gallic horse, killing 74. The next day the German leaders came to Caesar's camp to apologise and seek an extension of the truce. Caesar detained them and attacked the leaderless German camp. The Germans, taken by surprise, fled to the confluence of the Meuse and Rhine, where most were killed or drowned; women and children were hunted down by the cavalry. Caesar claims that not a single Roman was killed.

In Rome, when Caesar's dispatch arrived and the Senate proposed a thanksgiving, Cato moved that Caesar be handed over to the Germans to expiate the breach of faith and to avert divine punishment from Rome. Plutarch and Appian, drawing on a hostile tradition, report his speech. It was a striking moment, though the motion had no chance of passing.

Modern scholars regard the episode as one of the darkest in Caesar's career and possibly a genocide. Recent archaeological work at Kessel in the Netherlands, where large quantities of human bones, weapons and Late Iron Age material were dredged from the Maas, has been linked to the massacre, though the identification is debated.
set.debate: The identification of the Kessel finds with the battle site, and Caesar's population figure, are disputed.

scholarship: Roymans, 'A Roman massacre in the far north', in Fernández-Götz and Roymans (eds.), Conflict Archaeology (2018)
Powell, 'Julius Caesar and his presentation of massacre', in Welch and Powell (eds.), Julius Caesar as Artful Reporter (1998)

set.detail:
Late in summer 55, after his Rhine bridge, Caesar decided on an expedition to Britain, justifying it by British help to the Gauls and his ignorance of the island, which Gallic traders would not explain. He sent Commius, king of the Atrebates, to persuade British tribes to submit, and Gaius Volusenus to reconnoitre the coast. With two legions, the Seventh and Tenth, in eighty transports, he sailed from the territory of the Morini, probably from near Boulogne, around midnight on 24/25 August, arriving off the cliffs of Dover the next morning to find the Britons waiting.

He moved seven miles along the coast to an open shore, probably near Deal or Walmer, but the ships could not come close inshore, and the legionaries hesitated to jump into deep water under attack, until the standard-bearer of the Tenth leapt overboard, calling on his comrades not to betray the eagle. The landing succeeded after hard fighting. The eighteen transports carrying the cavalry were scattered by storms, and a high tide at full moon wrecked many of the beached warships and transports. The Britons attacked a foraging party of the Seventh legion; Caesar rescued it and defeated them again.

Lacking cavalry and supplies, and with the equinox approaching, Caesar accepted hostages from some tribes and returned to Gaul after about three weeks. The expedition achieved little militarily, but in Rome the news caused a sensation; the Senate voted a twenty-day thanksgiving. Catullus refers to Caesar crossing to the 'remotest Britons'.

The invasion was primarily a reconnaissance and a propaganda success. Recent work at Ebbsfleet in Kent has identified a large defensive ditch of mid-first-century BC date that some archaeologists link to Caesar's second expedition of 54.
set.debate: The landing site (Deal, Walmer or Pegwell Bay) is disputed.

scholarship: Creighton, Coins and Power in Late Iron Age Britain (2000)

set.detail:
In autumn 54, because of a poor harvest, Caesar dispersed his eight and a half legions in winter camps across northern Gaul. One legion and five cohorts, about 9,000 men under the legates Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta, wintered at Atuatuca in the territory of the Eburones. Fifteen days after their arrival, the Eburones under Ambiorix and Catuvolcus attacked the camp. Repulsed, Ambiorix asked for a parley and told the legates that all Gaul was rising, that a large German force had crossed the Rhine, and that he would give them safe passage to another camp.

At a council of war Cotta and most officers argued for staying; Sabinus insisted on leaving, and after a night of argument his view prevailed. At dawn the column marched out, strung out in a long line with heavy baggage. Two miles from camp, in a deep valley, the Eburones ambushed it. The Romans formed a circle and fought from early morning until late afternoon. Sabinus went to negotiate with Ambiorix and was killed; Cotta died fighting, wounded in the face by a sling bullet. The survivors fought their way back to the camp, where the standard-bearer Lucius Petrosidius threw the eagle over the rampart before he died, and that night they killed themselves. Only a few escaped to Labienus.

The disaster was the worst Roman defeat of the Gallic War. Caesar grew his hair and beard in mourning until he avenged it. Ambiorix went on to attack Quintus Cicero's camp among the Nervii, which Caesar relieved. In 53 Caesar devastated the land of the Eburones, inviting neighbouring tribes to plunder it, but Ambiorix escaped.

Caesar's account blames Sabinus and praises Cotta, perhaps to shift responsibility from his own decision to disperse the army. The site of Atuatuca is uncertain; Tongeren has been suggested but is disputed.
set.debate: Site uncertain (Tongeren, the Geer valley, or elsewhere in the Eburones' territory).

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)

set.detail:
Crassus, governor of Syria with seven legions, about 4,000 cavalry including 1,000 Gauls under his son Publius, and 4,000 light troops, crossed the Euphrates at Zeugma in spring 53 and, advised by the Osroenian chieftain Abgar (Ariamnes), struck across the Mesopotamian steppe toward Seleucia instead of following the river or going through Armenia as Artavasdes urged. Orodes II invaded Armenia, while his general, the Suren of the Parthian noble house, met Crassus near the river Balissus south of Carrhae with 1,000 cataphracts, heavily armoured cavalry, and 9,000 horse archers.

The Romans formed a hollow square. The horse archers, resupplied with arrows from a train of 1,000 camels, shot into it from a distance, while the cataphracts threatened any attempt to break out. Publius Crassus charged with the cavalry and eight cohorts; he was lured away, surrounded and killed, and his head was brought back on a spear and displayed before his father. The army held until nightfall, then abandoned 4,000 wounded and retreated to Carrhae. The next night they tried to escape north toward the Armenian hills.

Days later, near Sinnaca, Crassus was forced by his mutinous troops to accept the Suren's invitation to negotiate and was killed in a scuffle. Of perhaps 40,000 Romans, 20,000 died and 10,000 were captured and settled at Merv; Cassius escaped with 500 horse and organised the defence of Syria. Seven legionary eagles were lost.

Carrhae was one of the worst defeats in Roman history, a revenge that dominated Roman foreign policy until Augustus recovered the standards diplomatically in 20 BC. It also removed Crassus from the triumvirate, leaving Pompey and Caesar face to face. Orodes, jealous of his victorious general, had the Suren executed soon after.
set.debate: Plutarch's narrative may draw on a Parthian-sympathetic or Cassian source; the date is uncertain, early summer 53. Roman numbers, the exact site and the date (traditionally 9 June, from Ovid's Fasti 6.465) are discussed.

scholarship: Traina, Carrhae (2010)
Weggen, Der Lange Schatten von Carrhae (2011)

set.detail:
On 18 January 52 Publius Clodius, candidate for the praetorship, was returning to Rome along the Via Appia from Aricia with about thirty armed slaves when he met Titus Annius Milo, candidate for the consulship, travelling with his wife and a larger retinue including gladiators, near the shrine of Bona Dea at Bovillae. A brawl broke out at the rear of the column; Clodius was wounded by a gladiator's spear and carried into a nearby inn. Milo, judging it safer to kill him than leave him alive, had him dragged out and killed. His body was left on the road until a passing senator brought it to Rome.

The next day the Clodian mob, led by Sextus Cloelius, carried the body into the Senate house, the Curia Hostilia, built a pyre from its benches, tables and the record books, and cremated Clodius there. The fire spread to the Curia and the adjacent Basilica Porcia, destroying both. Riots continued for days; the mob attacked the house of the interrex Marcus Lepidus and demanded that Pompey take the consulship or dictatorship.

The Senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum, instructing Pompey and the tribunes to protect the state, and Pompey levied troops throughout Italy. In February Pompey was made sole consul. Milo was tried in April under Pompey's new law on violence, in a court guarded by troops, and convicted; he went into exile at Massilia.

Asconius' commentary on Cicero's Pro Milone gives a detailed account based on the official records, making the murder one of the best-documented events of the Republic. It ended six years of gang warfare and paved the way for Pompey's realignment with the optimates.

scholarship: Lintott, 'Cicero and Milo', JRS 64 (1974)

set.detail:
With no consuls elected for 52, the city in chaos after Clodius' murder, and calls for Pompey's dictatorship, Bibulus proposed and Cato supported that Pompey be elected sole consul, 'consul sine collega', an unprecedented office. Cato explained that any government was better than none, and that a sole consul was bound by law as a dictator was not. The interrex Servius Sulpicius declared Pompey elected on 24 Intercalaris (late February) 52. He retained his proconsular command in Spain at the same time.

Pompey acted swiftly. He passed a law on violence (lex Pompeia de vi) and a law on bribery with simplified procedures, limited speaking times, and juries selected from a list of 360 approved by him. Milo was convicted, and many others were condemned for bribery. He passed the law of the ten tribunes permitting Caesar to stand in absence, then a law requiring candidates to stand in person (lex de iure magistratuum), to which he added a clause exempting Caesar. His lex de provinciis imposed a five-year interval between office and provincial command.

In August Pompey took as colleague his new father-in-law, Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio, whose daughter Cornelia he had married, widowed by Publius Crassus' death at Carrhae. Scipio himself was under prosecution for bribery, and Pompey's protection of him undermined his own reforms. His imperium in Spain was extended for five years.

The sole consulship marked Pompey's realignment toward the optimates and away from Caesar, especially after Julia's death in 54 and Crassus' in 53. Modern scholars see it as a step toward the principate, combining a consulship with a provincial command governed by legates, which Augustus would make permanent.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)

set.detail:
In winter 53/52, with Caesar in Cisalpine Gaul and the news from Rome of Clodius' murder suggesting he might be detained there, Gallic leaders met secretly in the forests and agreed to rise. Resentment at the execution of Acco and at Roman demands was intense. The Carnutes, whose territory contained the sacred place where the druids met annually, volunteered to strike first. On a fixed day, probably in January 52, they entered Cenabum (Orléans), their chief town and a major trading centre on the Loire, under Gutruatus and Conconnetodumnus, and massacred all the Roman citizens there, including the equestrian Gaius Fufius Cita, who managed the grain supply for Caesar.

The news spread across Gaul by shouting from field to field, reaching the Arverni, 160 miles away, before the end of the first watch of the night. There the young noble Vercingetorix, whose father Celtillus had been killed for seeking kingship, raised his clients, was expelled by his uncle Gobannitio and the Arvernian nobles, then returned with a force of the poor and dispossessed, seized power at Gergovia, and was proclaimed king. Within weeks the Senones, Parisii, Pictones, Cadurci, Turoni, Aulerci, Lemovices and Andes had joined him, and he was made supreme commander.

Caesar returned in midwinter, crossed the Cevennes through deep snow, and drove north to rejoin his legions. In revenge he took Cenabum after a brief siege, burned it and gave its plunder to his soldiers.

The massacre marked the start of the general revolt of 52, the most dangerous crisis of Caesar's command. Modern historians stress that it was the result of long-term resentment and the political rise of a new Gallic leadership.

scholarship: Goudineau, César et la Gaule (1990)
Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)

set.detail:
Vercingetorix's strategy in 52 was to starve Caesar by burning towns and farms in his path, and over twenty towns of the Bituriges were burned in a single day. The Bituriges, however, begged him to spare Avaricum (Bourges), their capital and one of the finest cities in Gaul, protected by marshes and a river on almost all sides, with only a narrow approach. Vercingetorix reluctantly agreed and camped sixteen miles away to harass Caesar's foragers.

Caesar besieged Avaricum for twenty-seven days in late winter and early spring. His soldiers, short of food, refused his offer to lift the siege. Across the narrow approach they built a siege terrace 330 feet wide and 80 feet high, with two towers. The Gauls, experienced miners, undermined the terrace and set it on fire; their walls, a distinctive construction of alternating timber beams and stone, the murus gallicus that Caesar describes in detail, resisted battering rams and fire.

During a heavy rainstorm, when the guards were careless, Caesar ordered an assault; the legionaries scaled the walls and took the city. Enraged by the massacre at Cenabum and the hardships of the siege, they spared no one: of some 40,000 inhabitants, only 800 escaped to Vercingetorix. The army found abundant grain, which sustained it for the rest of the campaign.

Vercingetorix turned the defeat to advantage, arguing that he had opposed defending the town; his prestige increased, and new tribes joined him. Excavations in Bourges have revealed remains of the murus gallicus and the city's Iron Age defences, confirming aspects of Caesar's description.
set.debate: The figure of 40,000 killed is Caesar's and likely exaggerated.

scholarship: Goudineau, César et la Gaule (1990)
Ralston, Celtic Fortifications (2006)

set.detail:
After Avaricum, Caesar divided his army: Labienus took four legions against the Senones and Parisii, while Caesar marched with six legions to Gergovia, the Arvernian stronghold on a plateau 700 metres above the Allier plain south of modern Clermont-Ferrand. Vercingetorix had camped his army on the slopes below the walls. Caesar built a large camp and a smaller one on a hill opposite, linked by a double ditch, and tried to cut the defenders' water supply.

During the siege the Aeduan contingent marching to join Caesar was led into revolt by Litaviccus; Caesar intercepted it with four legions, leaving only two in camp, which barely held against a Gallic attack. On his return, noticing that the Gauls had concentrated on fortifying the western ridge, Caesar planned a limited assault on the southern side to capture the Gallic camps below the walls. The attack succeeded, but the legions, carried away by enthusiasm, did not hear the recall and pressed on to the town wall itself. Women on the walls threw down clothes and silver, begging for mercy. Then the Gallic army returned, and the arrival of Aeduan allies on the Roman flank, mistaken for enemies, threw the Romans into confusion. They were driven back with the loss of 46 centurions and nearly 700 soldiers.

The centurion Lucius Fabius, who had sworn to be the first on the walls, was killed there, and Marcus Petronius died holding the gate to save his men. Caesar reproached his soldiers for their recklessness, and withdrew. The defeat shattered his reputation for invincibility; the Aedui defected, and much of Gaul followed.

Excavations in the 1990s and 2000s on the plateau of Gergovie and at La Roche-Blanche confirmed the location of Caesar's camps and ditches. A sword said to have been lost by Caesar was displayed by the Arverni in a temple.

scholarship: Goudineau, César et la Gaule (1990)

set.detail:
After the cavalry battle in the Vingeanne, Vercingetorix withdrew with 80,000 men into Alesia, an oppidum of the Mandubii on Mont Auxois above the modern village of Alise-Sainte-Reine in Burgundy. Caesar, with some ten legions and auxiliaries, perhaps 60,000-70,000 men, decided to besiege it. He built an inner line of fortifications (contravallation) eleven miles long to trap the defenders, with ditches, a rampart and towers, and booby traps: pits with sharpened stakes (lilia), buried stakes with iron hooks (stimuli) and abatis (cippi). Then, learning that Vercingetorix had sent his cavalry to raise a relief army, he built an outer line of fourteen miles (circumvallation) facing outward.

Inside Alesia food ran out. The Mandubii expelled their women and children, but Caesar refused to let them pass, and they died between the lines. The relief army, said by Caesar to number 250,000 foot and 8,000 horse under four commanders including Commius and Vercassivellaunus, arrived and attacked the outer lines for three days, while Vercingetorix attacked from inside. The decisive assault came on the weak point of the northern lines on Mont Réa, where Vercassivellaunus led 60,000 picked men. Labienus held with six cohorts, then reinforcements; Caesar, conspicuous in his scarlet cloak, led a counterattack, and his cavalry attacked the Gauls from behind. The relief army was routed.

The next day Vercingetorix surrendered. Plutarch and Dio describe him riding out in his finest armour, circling Caesar's tribunal, then throwing down his arms and sitting at Caesar's feet. He was taken to Rome, held for six years, displayed in Caesar's triumph of 46, and executed.

Excavations under Napoleon III (1861-65) and a Franco-German project (1991-97) at Alise-Sainte-Reine identified the ditches, camps, traps and weapons, confirming the site against rival claims (notably Chaux-des-Crotenay in the Jura).
set.debate: Caesar's relief-army figure is almost certainly exaggerated. Site identification at Alise-Sainte-Reine is generally accepted; Caesar's figures for the relief army are not.

scholarship: Reddé and von Schnurbein (eds.), Alésia: fouilles et recherches franco-allemandes (2001)
Reddé, Alésia: l'archéologie face à l'imaginaire (2003)

set.detail:
Throughout 50 the question of Caesar's recall paralysed Roman politics. The consul Gaius Claudius Marcellus and the optimates sought to name a successor to Caesar's Gallic provinces; the tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio, now in Caesar's pay, vetoed every attempt, proposing instead that Caesar and Pompey both give up their armies simultaneously. The proposal was popular, as it seemed to offer peace.

On 1 December 50 Marcellus put two questions to the Senate separately. On whether Caesar should be replaced, the Senate voted yes; on whether Pompey should be replaced, it voted no. Curio then demanded a vote on whether both should lay down their commands. The Senate voted 370 to 22 in favour. Marcellus dismissed the meeting, saying 'Have it your way: Caesar as your master!' The crowd showered Curio with flowers.

The next day, on a false rumour that Caesar was marching on Italy with ten legions, Marcellus went to Pompey's villa outside the city with the consuls-designate, handed him a sword, and asked him to take command of the two legions at Capua (those withdrawn from Caesar for the Parthian war) and raise more troops in defence of the state. Pompey accepted, 'unless something better could be found'. Curio's tribunate ended on 9 December; he went to Caesar at Ravenna and returned to Rome on 1 January 49 with Caesar's last offer.

The vote of 1 December shows that most senators wanted peace and were willing to strip both dynasts of power, but a small group of optimates, led by Cato, Marcellus and Lentulus Crus, preferred war to compromise. Modern accounts (Morstein-Marx, Raaflaub) emphasise this vote as evidence that the civil war was not inevitable.

scholarship: Raaflaub, Dignitatis contentio (1974)

set.detail:
On 1 January 49 Curio delivered Caesar's letter to the new consuls, Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Crus and Gaius Claudius Marcellus. The tribunes Mark Antony and Quintus Cassius forced its reading: Caesar listed his services and offered to lay down his command if Pompey did the same, failing which he would defend his rights and the state's liberty. The consuls refused a debate on it. Metellus Scipio, speaking for Pompey, proposed that Caesar be ordered to disband his army by a fixed date or be considered a public enemy; Antony and Cassius vetoed it.

Private negotiations continued for a week. Caesar, through his friends and through Cicero, who had just returned from Cilicia hoping for a triumph, reduced his demands to keeping Illyricum and one legion until his consulship; Pompey seemed willing, but Lentulus, Cato and Marcellus refused. On 7 January the Senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum, instructing the consuls, praetors, tribunes and proconsuls near the city, that is Pompey, to see that the state came to no harm. Antony and Cassius, warned that their safety could not be guaranteed, fled the city disguised as slaves in a hired carriage, with Curio and Caelius, to join Caesar at Ravenna.

The Senate then assigned provinces: Domitius Ahenobarbus to succeed Caesar in Transalpine Gaul, Considius Nonianus in the Cisalpina, Metellus Scipio to Syria, and others. Levies were ordered throughout Italy, and money was voted to Pompey from the treasury.

Caesar used the treatment of the tribunes as his justification for invasion: the sacrosanctity of the tribunate had been violated, as in Sulla's time. His own account in the Civil War opens with this narrative, placing responsibility on the intransigence of a small faction. Modern historians debate the balance of responsibility; Raaflaub emphasises Caesar's concern for his dignitas, others the optimates' determination to destroy him.

scholarship: Raaflaub, Dignitatis contentio (1974)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

set.detail:
On the night of 10/11 January 49 by the unreformed calendar (late November in solar terms), Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the small river that marked the boundary between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper, with the Thirteenth legion. Leading an army out of his province without the Senate's authority was treason under Sulla's lex Cornelia de maiestate. He had spent the day publicly at Ravenna, attending a show and a dinner, before slipping away in a carriage drawn by mules from a nearby bakery, losing his way in the dark before finding the road.

Suetonius' account, probably from Asinius Pollio, who was present, describes Caesar hesitating at the bridge, saying to his companions that turning back was still possible but crossing meant war. Then a figure of extraordinary size and beauty appeared, playing a reed pipe; shepherds and soldiers gathered to listen, and he seized a trumpet from a soldier and sounded the advance as he crossed. Caesar exclaimed, 'Let us go where the signs of the gods and the injustice of our enemies call us. The die is cast.' Plutarch, also following Pollio, says Caesar spoke in Greek, quoting Menander: 'anerriphtho kubos', let the die be thrown.

Caesar himself does not mention the Rubicon in his Civil War; he simply says he addressed his soldiers at Ravenna and marched to Ariminum. The silence was deliberate: the crossing was the moment of illegality.

The identification of the river is uncertain. In 1933 Mussolini officially identified it with the Fiumicino near Savignano, renamed Rubicone, but the Pisciatello and the Uso have also been proposed. The phrase 'crossing the Rubicon' became proverbial for an irrevocable decision.
set.debate: Exact date (10 or 11 January by the pre-Julian calendar; about late November 50 in Julian terms). The river's identity (Fiumicino, Pisciatello or Uso), and whether Caesar's words were Latin or Greek, are debated.

scholarship: Beard, 'The Rubicon', in SPQR (2015)
Pelling, Plutarch: Caesar (2011)

set.detail:
After securing Italy and Rome in 49, Caesar marched to Spain to destroy Pompey's legions there, 'going against an army without a general, before turning against a general without an army'. Pompey's legates Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius, with five legions plus Spanish auxiliaries, had concentrated at Ilerda (Lleida), a town on a hill above the river Sicoris (Segre). Caesar's legate Gaius Fabius arrived first with three legions, and Caesar joined in June with 900 cavalry.

The campaign was one of manoeuvre. An early Caesarian attempt to seize a hill between Ilerda and the Pompeian camp failed. Then floods swept away the bridges over the Sicoris, cutting Caesar off from his supplies; a large supply convoy from Gaul was nearly lost, and grain prices in his camp soared. In Rome the Pompeians celebrated. Caesar built boats of wicker and hides, on the British model, and established a new bridgehead upstream; his cavalry then harried the Pompeian foragers.

The Pompeians tried to withdraw south across the Ebro to Celtiberia. Caesar's men forded the Sicoris neck-deep, with the cavalry breaking the current, and overtook them in the hills. He refused to fight, despite his soldiers' eagerness, preferring to cut them off from water. Soldiers of the two armies began to fraternise, until Petreius massacred Caesarians in his camp. Finally, short of water and food, Afranius and Petreius surrendered on 2 August 49.

Caesar released the Pompeian soldiers, disbanding some and letting others return to Italy, and pardoned the commanders, who went straight to Pompey. Ilerda was a masterpiece of bloodless strategy and a propaganda triumph for Caesar's clemency. Further Spain, under Varro, surrendered soon after.

scholarship: Carter, Julius Caesar: The Civil War Books I and II (1991)

set.detail:
After crossing to Epirus in January 48 and receiving Antony's reinforcements in spring, Caesar, with some 22,000 men, confronted Pompey, whose army of perhaps 45,000 was encamped on the coast near Dyrrachium (Durrës), supplied by sea. Caesar attempted the extraordinary feat of besieging a larger army: he built a line of fortifications some seventeen miles long around Pompey's position on the hills south of the town, while Pompey built an inner line of fifteen miles. Caesar's men, short of grain, made bread from a root called chara, which they threw into Pompey's lines to show they could eat anything.

Pompey's cavalry suffered for lack of fodder, and his army from lack of water, as Caesar diverted the streams. But in July, informed by two Allobrogian deserters of a weak point at the southern end of Caesar's line near the sea, Pompey launched a combined land and sea attack. The Ninth legion was overwhelmed; Caesar's counterattack with thirty-three cohorts went astray in the maze of fortifications and was routed. Caesar lost 960 men and 32 military tribunes and centurions, and 32 standards. He seized a standard-bearer to halt the flight, and the man tried to strike him.

Caesar said afterward that the war would have been over that day if the enemy had had a commander who knew how to win; Pompey, suspecting a trap, did not pursue. Labienus executed the Caesarian prisoners. Caesar retreated to Apollonia and then into Thessaly to join Domitius Calvinus and find supplies, sacking Gomphi.

Dyrrachium encouraged the Pompeian leadership to press Pompey for a decisive battle, which led to Pharsalus. Their overconfidence was fatal: senators quarrelled over Caesar's priesthood and confiscated properties before the battle.
set.debate: Casualty figures are Caesar's own; Orosius gives 4,000 dead.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

set.detail:
On 9 August 48 (by the unreformed calendar, about 7 June solar), on the plain of Pharsalus in Thessaly near the river Enipeus, Pompey, pressed by his senatorial advisers, offered battle. He had about 45,000 legionaries in 110 cohorts and 7,000 cavalry; Caesar, 22,000 legionaries in 80 cohorts and 1,000 cavalry. Pompey anchored his right on the river and massed his cavalry under Labienus on the left, planning to sweep around Caesar's right flank and roll up his line. He ordered his infantry to stand and receive the Caesarian charge rather than advance, to tire the enemy.
