Caesar anticipated the plan. He took one cohort from the third line of each legion to form a fourth line of six cohorts, hidden behind his right-wing cavalry, with orders to use their pila as spears against the faces of the cavalry. When Labienus' horsemen drove back Caesar's cavalry, the fourth line charged; the inexperienced Pompeian horsemen, many young aristocrats, fled to the hills. The cohorts then turned on Pompey's archers and slingers and attacked the left flank of his infantry. Caesar's veterans, having halted in the middle of their charge to recover their breath when they saw Pompey's men stand, threw their pila and engaged. Caesar then committed his third line, and the Pompeian army collapsed.

Caesar claims he lost 200 men and 30 centurions; the Pompeians 15,000 dead and 24,000 captured. Asinius Pollio, present, gave 6,000 Pompeian dead. Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus was killed. Caesar, viewing the dead, said: 'They wanted it; after such deeds, I, Gaius Caesar, would have been condemned had I not sought help from my army.' He pardoned most prisoners, including Brutus, and burned Pompey's correspondence unread.

Pompey fled to the coast and sailed for Egypt. Pharsalus effectively decided the civil war, though resistance continued in Africa and Spain.
set.debate: Battlefield location; Caesar's numbers (especially Pompeian losses) versus Pollio's. The battlefield's location north or south of the Enipeus is disputed; Caesar's casualty figures are certainly too low for his side.

scholarship: Pelling, Plutarch: Caesar (2011)

set.detail:
After Pharsalus Pompey fled via Larisa and Amphipolis to Mytilene, where he collected his wife Cornelia and his son Sextus, and then along the coast of Asia Minor to Cyprus. Rejecting Parthia and Juba, he decided to seek refuge in Egypt, whose young king, Ptolemy XIII, owed his throne to Pompey's support of Ptolemy XII. He arrived off Pelusium on 28 September 48, where the boy king's army was facing that of his sister Cleopatra.

The king's advisers, the eunuch Pothinus, the general Achillas and the rhetorician Theodotus of Chios, debated whether to receive him. Theodotus argued that a dead man does not bite; to receive Pompey would make Caesar an enemy, to refuse him would make Pompey one. They sent a small boat with Achillas and two Roman officers, Lucius Septimius, a former centurion of Pompey's, and Salvius. As Pompey stepped ashore, Septimius stabbed him in the back; Pompey covered his face with his toga and died without a word, on the day after his fifty-eighth birthday. Cornelia watched from the ship. His head was cut off and preserved; his body was left on the beach, where his freedman Philippus burned it on a pyre made from a broken boat.

When Caesar arrived in Alexandria a few days later, Theodotus presented the head and Pompey's signet ring, showing a lion holding a sword. Caesar wept and turned away, ordered the head buried in a shrine of Nemesis near the city, and had Pompey's killers put to death in time. Theodotus fled and was later executed by Brutus.

Pompey's death became a moral exemplum of the reversal of fortune. Cicero commented that he could not doubt how Pompey's life would end; Lucan made the scene the centrepiece of Book 8. His ashes were returned to Cornelia, who buried them at his Alban villa.
set.debate: Date: Velleius and Plutarch agree on the day after his birthday (29 September, unreformed calendar).

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2002)

set.detail:
Caesar landed at Alexandria in early October 48 with only 3,200 infantry and 800 cavalry. He insisted on settling the dispute between Ptolemy XIII and Cleopatra under Ptolemy XII's will, and demanded repayment of the old debts. After Cleopatra's arrival and his decision in her favour, the Alexandrians and Ptolemy's army of 20,000 under Achillas, including many of Gabinius' former soldiers settled in Egypt, rose against him. Caesar was besieged in the palace quarter for some six months.

Caesar fortified the palace and the theatre, burned the Egyptian fleet in the harbour, with the fire spreading to the docks and possibly to warehouses of books, and seized the Pharos lighthouse. Cleopatra's younger sister Arsinoe escaped to the Egyptian army, was proclaimed queen, and had Achillas killed by her eunuch Ganymedes, who took command. Ganymedes tried to poison Caesar's water by pumping seawater into the cisterns; Caesar dug new wells. Caesar released Ptolemy XIII, who had been his hostage, hoping he would end the war, but he joined the Egyptian forces.

In a battle for the Heptastadion, the mole linking the Pharos to the mainland, Caesar's men were routed and he had to swim for safety. Reinforcements came from Asia: the Thirty-Seventh legion, formed from Pompey's surrendered troops, and a relief army under Mithridates of Pergamon, with 3,000 Jews under Antipater. Mithridates took Pelusium and marched up the Delta; Caesar joined him, and in March 47 they defeated the Egyptian army at the battle of the Nile, where Ptolemy XIII drowned.

The Alexandrian War was described in the Bellum Alexandrinum, probably by Hirtius. It was the most dangerous episode of Caesar's career after Dyrrachium, entered into, his critics thought, for Cleopatra's sake.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Antony and Cleopatra (2010)
Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001)

set.detail:
While Caesar was trapped in Alexandria, Pharnaces II, son of Mithridates and king of the Bosporus, exploited the civil war to reconquer his father's kingdom of Pontus and invade Lesser Armenia and Cappadocia. At Nicopolis in late 48 he defeated Caesar's legate Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, whose army included Deiotarus' legions trained in the Roman manner, and then occupied Pontus, castrating Roman captives and massacring Romans at Amisus.

Caesar, after settling Egypt and Syria, marched rapidly through Cilicia and Cappadocia in summer 47, collecting troops: the veteran Sixth legion, reduced to under 1,000 men, Deiotarus' legion, and two others. Pharnaces, sending envoys and offering terms, tried to delay him; Caesar refused. Pharnaces took position on a hill near Zela in Pontus, the scene of his father's victory over Triarius in 67. On 2 August 47, while the Romans were fortifying a camp on the opposite hill, Pharnaces attacked uphill with scythed chariots and infantry. The surprised Romans recovered, the Sixth legion broke the Pontic line, and the army was routed within four hours. Pharnaces fled to the Bosporus, where he was killed by his governor Asander.

Caesar wrote to his friend Matius in Rome 'veni, vidi, vici', I came, I saw, I conquered; in his Pontic triumph the next year the words were displayed on a placard. He also remarked on Pompey's good luck in having won his reputation against such enemies.

The battle restored Roman control in Anatolia. Caesar rewarded Mithridates of Pergamon with the Bosporan kingdom and part of Galatia, and confirmed the arrangements of the client kings, fining those who had supported Pompey, including Deiotarus.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

set.detail:
In Africa the Pompeians regrouped under Metellus Scipio, with Labienus, Afranius, Petreius, and King Juba I of Numidia, with ten legions, 15,000 cavalry, light troops and 120 elephants. Caesar landed near Hadrumetum in late December 47 with too few troops and was nearly defeated at Ruspina in January 46. After months of manoeuvre in Byzacena, reinforced to ten legions, he besieged Thapsus, a coastal town on a narrow isthmus between the sea and a salt lagoon, to force Scipio to battle.

On 6 April 46 Scipio and Juba approached in two groups to relieve the town and began fortifying positions. Caesar deployed his legions in three lines, with five cohorts of the Fifth legion on each wing to face the elephants, which they had trained to fight using elephants imported from Italy. Before Caesar gave the signal, a trumpeter on the right, urged on by the eager veterans, sounded the attack. Caesar, seeing that he could not stop it, spurred his horse into the charge. Slingers and archers stampeded the elephants on the Pompeian left, which trampled their own men; a wounded elephant attacked a camp follower and was killed by a soldier of the Fifth, which afterwards bore an elephant on its standards.

The Pompeian army collapsed. Caesar's veterans, embittered by years of war, massacred those who tried to surrender, ignoring his orders; the Bellum Africum gives 10,000 Pompeian dead, against 50 Caesarians. Plutarch reports a story that Caesar suffered an epileptic seizure at the start of the battle and took no part.

Thapsus destroyed the Pompeian cause in Africa. Cato killed himself at Utica, Juba and Petreius killed each other, Scipio drowned himself, Afranius was killed. Labienus and Pompey's sons escaped to Spain.
set.debate: The epileptic seizure story in Plutarch and the casualty figures are uncertain.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

set.detail:
Marcus Porcius Cato commanded the Pompeian garrison at Utica, the capital of the province of Africa, during the campaign of 46, having led the remnants of Pompey's fleet from Corcyra and marched an army across the desert of Libya from Cyrenaica in thirty days. When news of Thapsus arrived, he tried to organise resistance among the 300 Roman merchants and senators in Utica, then, seeing that they wanted to surrender, helped them escape by sea and refused to seek Caesar's pardon himself, saying he would not accept a favour from a tyrant who had no right to grant it.

On the night of his death, in mid-April 46, he dined with friends and discussed the Stoic paradox that only the good man is free. He then retired and read Plato's Phaedo, on the immortality of the soul, twice. Finding his sword had been removed by his son, he demanded it back; at dawn he stabbed himself in the stomach. His doctor found him still alive and bandaged the wound, but Cato tore it open with his hands and died. He was forty-eight.

Caesar, on hearing the news, said: 'Cato, I begrudge you your death, as you begrudged me the chance to save your life.' The people of Utica buried him with honour and set up a statue of him with a sword.

Cato's death made him the martyr of the Republic. Cicero wrote a eulogy, Cato, Brutus another, and Caesar replied with the Anticato. Lucan made him the moral hero of the Pharsalia, Seneca the model Stoic sage, and Virgil placed him giving laws to the righteous in Elysium. In later centuries he became a symbol of republican virtue and resistance to tyranny, as in Addison's Cato (1713), admired by George Washington.

scholarship: Goar, The Legend of Cato Uticensis (1987)
Morrell, Pompey, Cato, and the Governance of the Roman Empire (2017)

set.detail:
Between late July and early September 46, Caesar celebrated four triumphs on separate days over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa. He did not triumph over Roman citizens, framing the African victory as over Juba. The Gallic triumph displayed Vercingetorix, who was then executed; his chariot's axle broke as it passed the temple of Fortuna, and Caesar climbed the Capitoline steps on his knees, flanked by elephants carrying torches. The Egyptian triumph displayed Arsinoe IV, whose presence moved the crowd to pity, and images of the Nile and the burning Pharos. The Pontic triumph carried the placard 'veni vidi vici'. The African triumph showed the young son of Juba, the future Juba II, and caused offence with images of the suicides of Scipio, Petreius and Cato.

Caesar's soldiers marched singing obscene songs, including 'Citizens, lock up your wives: we bring the bald adulterer' and verses about his supposed affair with Nicomedes of Bithynia. Each veteran received 5,000 denarii, centurions twice and tribunes four times as much; each citizen 400 sesterces, plus grain and oil. The triumphs brought 65,000 talents in coin, 2,822 golden crowns.

Spectacles followed: a feast at 22,000 tables, gladiatorial combats in the Forum, a mock naval battle on an artificial lake in the Campus Martius with Tyrian and Egyptian fleets, a battle between armies of 500 infantry, 30 cavalry and 20 elephants each in the Circus, and the first giraffe seen in Rome. A silk awning protected spectators. On the final day he dedicated the Forum Iulium and the temple of Venus Genetrix.

The triumphs announced Caesar's supremacy. The Senate had voted him a dictatorship for ten years, a forty-day supplicatio, and 72 lictors, three times the normal number.

scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Östenberg, Staging the World (2009)

set.detail:
The Roman Republican calendar had 355 days, kept in line with the solar year by intercalating a month of 22 or 23 days in some years, a decision left to the pontifices, who had manipulated or neglected it for political reasons. By 46 the calendar was about three months ahead of the seasons: the 'harvest festival' fell in spring. Caesar, as pontifex maximus and dictator, with the advice of the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes and the scribe Marcus Flavius, introduced a solar calendar of 365 days, with an extra day every fourth year inserted after 23 February (the sixth day before the Kalends of March doubled, hence 'bissextile').

To realign the calendar with the seasons, 46 was given 445 days, the 'year of confusion' (annus confusionis): the regular intercalary month after February, and two extra months between November and December, totalling 67 extra days. The new calendar began on 1 January 45. The ten days added to the shorter months were placed at the end so as not to disturb the dates of festivals.

After Caesar's death, the pontifices misinterpreted the rule and intercalated every third year (counting inclusively), so that by 9 BC there had been three extra leap days; Augustus suspended intercalation until AD 8. In 44 the month Quinctilis was renamed Iulius in Caesar's honour; Sextilis became Augustus in 8 BC.

The Julian calendar, with a year of 365.25 days, was about eleven minutes too long; by the sixteenth century the error amounted to ten days, which led to Pope Gregory XIII's reform of 1582. It remained in use in Russia until 1918 and in Orthodox churches. Cicero, told that the constellation Lyra would rise the next day, remarked: 'Yes, by edict.'

scholarship: Rüpke, The Roman Calendar from Numa to Constantine (2011)
Bennett, 'The early Augustan calendars in Rome and Egypt', ZPE 142 (2003)
